stories.author: qtqtqt
stories.title: GIMP now has UI tests
stories.groq_label: GIMP implements automated UI tests to detect interface regressions early.
stories.groq_explain:
The announcement explains that GIMP now includes an automated graphical user interface (UI) testing platform. Because GIMP’s menus, dialogs and tools are tightly interlinked, changes to one part of the interface can unintentionally break another, and such problems may only be noticed after a user reports them. The new UI tests run each time contributor changes are merged, allowing developers to catch interface regressions early.

The article distinguishes UI tests from existing unit tests. Unit tests verify isolated pieces of code, such as the handling of XCF files, but they do not open a real window and therefore cannot confirm that dialogs appear or that menu actions work. Earlier GUI tests interacted directly with core code or simulated input events, yet they could not exercise the complete interface and were fragile. UI tests, by contrast, launch a full instance of GIMP, perform real user actions like clicking menus and buttons, and then examine the resulting state. If the outcome is incorrect the test fails and reports the problem.

At the time of writing, thirteen tests are in place. They verify that GIMP starts and shows its main window, that the Welcome dialog behaves correctly, that creating a new image, exporting a PNG, swapping colors, editing foreground colors, adding and deleting layers, undo and redo, zooming, selecting tools, using the bucket‑fill tool, saving preferences, and flattening an image all function as expected.

The tests are designed to run without a physical display. Each test creates a small hidden desktop environment, runs GIMP inside it, and then tears the environment down. To locate UI elements the tests rely on the accessibility data GIMP provides for screen readers, which also improves GIMP’s accessibility. The testing framework uses dogtail, a Python tool for UI automation. Because dogtail originally required a screen, the GIMP developers added a new feature to dogtail that enables headless operation; this contribution has been merged upstream so other projects can benefit. Currently the tests run only on Linux (both X11 and Wayland) because dogtail does not yet support Windows or macOS.

The article credits Harsh Verma for writing the UI tests and the dogtail enhancement, Jehan and Michal Odehnal for reviewing them, and points to the full merge request for more detail. It invites community involvement, noting that GIMP has many more dialogs and tools that could be covered. Developers are encouraged to write additional tests following the guide on the GIMP developer site, which explains how to create new tests and diagnose failures.

Overall, the introduction of UI tests represents a significant step toward more reliable releases, earlier bug detection, and better accessibility for GIMP users.

stories.author: JacobHenner
stories.title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)
stories.groq_label: Fixes CVE‑2026‑121481 buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock, adds input validation to EVP_DecodeBlock and corrects base64encode length check.
stories.groq_explain:
The page describes a pull request to the OpenSSL project that addresses a critical security flaw identified as CVE‑2026‑121481. The vulnerability is a buffer overflow in the function EVP_EncodeBlock, which can be triggered by invalid inputs and lead to undefined behavior or potential exploitation. The proposed changes resolve the overflow by returning ‑1 for invalid inputs and, in a later revision, by invoking OPENSSL_assert when such inputs are detected. The same defensive logic is applied to the related function EVP_DecodeBlock.

In addition to fixing the encoding and decoding functions, the patch corrects an incorrect length check in the base64encode routine found in http_client.c. The updates also include revisions to the documentation to reflect the new behavior, especially for zero‑length inputs, and new test cases that verify the fixes.

The discussion around the pull request shows a review timeline: an initial approval by a contributor named nhorman on November 11 2026, requests for changes on November 12 2026, a hold placed by bob‑beck for community consensus, and subsequent commits that refine the fix. Additional context mentions a related fuzzer commit and performance testing of the AVX2 encoder versus a scalar implementation, as well as versioning details for OpenSSL 4.1.0.

The significance of this change lies in preventing a high‑severity (CVSS 9.8) vulnerability that could allow attackers to cause memory corruption, crashes, or arbitrary code execution when OpenSSL processes malformed base64 data. By adding proper input validation, assertions, and documentation, the patch improves the security and robustness of OpenSSL’s base64 handling functions. The pull request has been merged, indicating that the fix is now part of the OpenSSL codebase.

stories.author: emot
stories.title: Vint Cerf on why TCP/IP was never patented
stories.groq_label: Vint Cerf says TCP/IP remains unpatented because it was deliberately kept open to ensure universal access and collaboration
stories.groq_explain:
The article announces the launch of a new technology and science podcast called Future Stories, whose first episode features an interview with Vint Cerf, the co‑designer of TCP/IP. The conversation, recorded over Zoom on October 14, runs about fifty‑six minutes and is available as a full audio file, a transcript, and short clips. Cerf, now 83, recently left Google after more than two decades and is helping to start a company called Tolero, which aims to build software for an interplanetary Internet, noting that “the speed of light is too slow.” He reflects on the open nature of the Internet, saying that because future allies cannot be predicted, the network must remain accessible to everyone.

During the interview Cerf shares several anecdotes that illustrate the collaborative spirit behind early networking work. He recounts a two‑week debugging effort that was solved in thirty seconds when his friend Steve Crocker identified the problem, emphasizing the value of teamwork. He also tells the story of how a commercial network in San Diego was named CERFnet after a naming conflict with a Dutch network; Cerf approved the use of his name despite initial hesitation and celebrated the launch by smashing a plastic bottle of glitter over a Cisco router. Another episode describes his attempt to link France’s Minitel service to MCI Mail, which ultimately failed, leaving him still puzzled.

The piece also mentions a humorous 1992 “IP on Everything” striptease photo Cerf posted in response to a question about his attire, and his concerns that future generations may be unable to interpret the digital records we leave behind. He shows a plaque from the original ARPANET Interface Message Processor, a large packet‑switching computer given to him when he left ARPA in 1982.

While AI is not a main focus of the interview, Cerf’s clear thinking on the topic is noted. The article provides links to the full conversation, the transcript, and a Portuguese write‑up, and invites listeners to subscribe, share, and suggest future guests. It also references a 2024 segment from Cerf’s earlier podcast that revisited the 1974 TCP paper by Cerf and Bob Kahn, explaining how TCP was later split into TCP and IP and became the core of the modern Internet launched by DARPA in 1983. The overall message underscores the importance of open, collaborative development in creating the enduring infrastructure of the Internet.

stories.author: cybermango
stories.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
stories.groq_label: Claude solved two longstanding black‑hole quantum‑gravity problems by completing a decades‑old phase‑transition calculation and finding the exact bound of a basic holographic test.
stories.groq_explain:
Claude, the Anthropic AI system, has resolved two long‑standing theoretical physics problems that involve black holes and the search for a quantum theory of gravity. The first problem concerned a phase transition that occurs when a theoretical universe is heated. At low temperature the universe contains a gas of particles, but above a certain temperature a black hole forms. Hawking and Page showed in 1983 that this transition is abrupt, but their calculation relied on general relativity, which breaks down when the universe becomes very small and spacetime loses a definite shape. In the quantum description of the same situation the transition was known to exist, yet it was unclear whether it was abrupt or smooth. In 2003 a group of physicists outlined the extremely complex calculation that would decide the question, but it was never completed. Claude assembled a small research group of copies of itself, solved nearly every component of the calculation independently, and cross‑checked the results against known limits. It demonstrated that the transition remains abrupt even in the regime where spacetime is fuzzy, indicating that the sudden formation of a black hole is a feature of the underlying quantum theory rather than an artifact of classical relativity.

The second problem involved a simplified model universe with two spatial dimensions. Physicists use a “bootstrap” approach to rule out inconsistent candidate theories of quantum gravity by establishing limits on the properties of black holes in that model. Since 2009 a numerical ceiling on the mass of the lightest black hole has been suggested, but a rigorous proof of the optimal ceiling has been missing, and the best proven bound fell short of the numerical evidence. Claude’s “Fable 5.2” identified a pattern in the numerical data that had been overlooked and applied a mathematical technique from another field to compute the exact ceiling for the simplest bootstrap method, proving that the bound cannot be lowered further. While this does not pinpoint the correct theory, it narrows the space of viable candidates.

Both findings do not describe our actual universe nor have immediate practical applications, but they advance the broader effort to reconcile quantum mechanics with general relativity. The article also explains that Claude’s work emerged from an experiment by Anthropic researcher Hongbin Chen, who asked the AI to list promising open problems in black‑hole physics. Claude produced a set of candidates, after which multiple AI agents worked in parallel, sharing progress and collaborating on related sub‑problems. The post links to the preprints where the detailed technical arguments are presented.

stories.author: D_R_Farrell
stories.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
stories.groq_label: Onlook is an open-source desktop tool that lets designers visually edit live codebases using AI agents.
stories.groq_explain: Onlook is an open‑source developer tool aimed at designers who want to create and edit real applications visually rather than through a terminal. It presents a live running version of a project on an infinite canvas, allowing designers to explore ideas side by side across mobile, tablet and desktop frames. The tool connects to existing AI coding assistants such as Claude Code, ChatGPT or Codex; users bring their own model credentials and the agent can edit the actual files in the project based on natural‑language prompts. Onlook works directly with any local Git repository: it launches the developer’s own dev server, displays the live app in the canvas, and tracks changes through Git. The application runs as a desktop, local‑first Electron app, so code never leaves the user’s machine and no cloud accounts or environment keys are required. Designers can export their work as self‑contained HTML, PNG, JPEG or PDF for hand‑off, review or sharing, and they can also generate pull requests from within the interface. The product supports parallel projects as tabs, safe work‑tree copies that keep the original folder untouched, and can import GitHub repositories or start new codebases from scratch. Onlook’s technology stack includes Electron, React 19, Zustand, CodeMirror and various tooling such as Bun and Turborepo. The project is released under the Apache 2.0 license, encouraging forks and customizations, and it gathers optional usage analytics to improve the app. By allowing designers to work directly on real codebases with AI assistance and visual feedback, Onlook aims to bridge the gap between design and development, reducing the need for separate mockup rebuilding and streamlining the hand‑off process.

stories.author: Terretta
stories.title: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
stories.groq_label: UK court orders the government to acknowledge it issued a secret Technical Capability Notice requiring Apple to modify iCloud encryption.
stories.groq_explain:
The article explains that the United Kingdom government has been compelled to admit that it issued Apple a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN) under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. A TCN is a confidential order that can require a technology company to modify its services to enable government surveillance. The existence of such an order had been denied by the government, which maintained a “neither confirm nor deny” stance, even though the order had been reported in the press. 

The dispute began after a Washington Post investigation in February 2025 revealed that the UK had ordered Apple to provide back‑door access to encrypted iCloud data, affecting users worldwide. In response, Apple withdrew its Advanced Data Protection (ADP) feature – an optional add‑on that extends end‑to‑end encryption so that Apple itself cannot decrypt the data – from new UK customers. Apple also stated it would not build any back‑door or master key, but was prohibited from mentioning the TCN publicly. The initial order was later withdrawn after diplomatic pressure, but a second TCN, reportedly limited to British users, was issued, prompting Apple to launch a fresh legal challenge in 2026. 

Civil‑rights groups Liberty and Privacy International, represented by Ben Jaffey KC, challenged the government’s secrecy at a hearing of the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September. They argued that keeping the order secret was untenable because its existence was already public and that the secrecy policy was damaging to justice. The government countered that disclosure could harm national security by revealing which companies were subject to such orders. The tribunal rejected that argument, ruling that the government had not shown any national‑security harm from acknowledging the notice. The tribunal did not decide whether the order was lawful or what technical changes were required, but it forced the government to admit the notice’s existence.

The article also highlights the practical impact of the dispute on users. Because Apple stopped offering ADP to new UK customers in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature retained it, while newer users could not. This created a “two‑tier” encryption system in which two people with identical iPhones and iCloud accounts – illustrated as fictional “Alice” (who enabled ADP) and “Bill” (who did not) – have different levels of protection. The author argues that this disparity undermines the expectation of uniform privacy for all users and raises broader concerns about government attempts to compel companies to weaken their own security measures. The significance of the tribunal’s decision lies in breaking the government’s secrecy shield, setting a precedent for greater transparency about surveillance orders, and exposing the tension between national‑security objectives and individual privacy rights.

stories.author: datascientist
stories.title: Pete warden on local AI, open models, voice interfaces, the future of hardware
stories.groq_label: Local AI is becoming more capable and economically viable, driving a shift from cloud to on-device models and new hardware.
stories.groq_explain:
The page presents a podcast episode titled “Pete Warden on Local AI, Open Models, Voice Interfaces, and the Future of Hardware.” In the interview, Ben Lorica talks with Pete Warden, a veteran deep‑learning engineer and co‑creator of the Moonshine Voice project, about why artificial intelligence is increasingly being run on devices rather than in cloud services. Warden explains that local AI has become far more capable than most people realize, noting that open‑weight models can now be quantized and run on laptops, browsers, and even small edge devices without a large loss of performance. He points out that the main obstacle to wider adoption is not technical but economic: cloud providers can monetize SaaS APIs, whereas locally running models give no direct revenue stream, so large companies have little incentive to market them.

The conversation covers several key themes. First, the rapid progress of open models means they are only a few months behind commercial offerings from firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI, and they are already competitive on benchmarks. Second, running AI locally can improve privacy, reduce latency, and enable voice as a more natural computing interface that goes beyond current assistants like Siri and Alexa. Warden emphasizes that low‑latency speech models are crucial for a good user experience, and that designing voice interfaces must account for failure and human feedback.

The interview also contrasts specialized speech models with end‑to‑end or multimodal approaches, arguing that specialized models can be more efficient for voice tasks. Warden discusses the economics of local AI, suggesting that as tools become easier to use—citing examples like Ollama—developers will find it viable to embed models directly into operating systems and applications. He highlights emerging hardware trends that could shift the AI landscape away from GPU‑centric inference, including high‑bandwidth flash storage and new processor designs from companies such as Apple and NVIDIA that are optimized for on‑device inference.

Overall, the episode argues that local AI is poised to become a mainstream alternative to cloud‑based services, driven by advances in open models, quantization techniques, and hardware. This shift matters because it promises greater user privacy, lower latency, and new business models that give enterprises more control over their AI workloads. The page includes a full transcript of the conversation, links to the video version, and references to related topics such as TinyML, sensor‑driven AI, and the broader debate over frontier AI regulation.

The article explains how to create an eight‑page foldable zine from a single A4 sheet and introduces a web tool called fanzines.app that simplifies the layout process. The author describes the traditional manual method: fold the A4 paper in half three times, cut along the center crease, and fold into a cross to produce a booklet without staples or glue, then fill it with photos, poems or notes. The difficulty with the conventional approach lies in arranging the flat sheet on a computer, because the pages must be placed in a non‑intuitive order and the top row needs to be printed upside down. To eliminate the need for rotating images and manually checking column order in graphics software, the author built fanzines.app, which lets users design each page right‑side up in the browser and automatically generates a 300 DPI PDF with the correct rotation and layout. All processing remains local, so no images are uploaded to a server.

Recent updates to the editor address several usability issues. The sidebar now groups page thumbnails into actual spreads that reflect how the physical booklet folds, and a new Spread view shows the facing page at lower opacity for easier alignment. Drag‑and‑drop support lets users import a folder of eight photos, with the interface indicating which pages will receive each image in reading order. The inspector has been streamlined: Fill, Fit and Center buttons replace manual coordinate entry, while precise numeric fields are still available in a collapsible section using millimetres for layout dimensions and points for text. Before exporting, a Review screen displays the full unfolded A4 sheet with optional cut and fold line overlays and a 5 mm safe margin that scales the layout to about 95 % to accommodate typical printer edge clipping. Additional enhancements include a mobile‑friendly interface that shows one page at a time with a bottom thumbnail strip, and bilingual support for English and Spanish, with language changes preserving the current work.

The article matters because it offers a practical, privacy‑preserving solution for anyone who wants to make small, self‑published booklets without the hassle of manual page ordering, making the creative process faster and more accessible on both desktop and mobile devices.

stories.author: notmine1337
stories.title: Someone reported java4shell bug in September 2026
stories.groq_label: A base64 decode stub in Java incorrectly handles inputs shorter than four bytes, causing negative output size and heap corruption and needing an early‑return fix
stories.groq_explain:
The pull request addresses a bug in the OpenJDK StubGenerator implementation for Base64 decoding on the x86_64 AVX‑512 VBMI code path. In the function generate_base64_decodeBlock, the variable L_finalBit processes leftover bytes ranging from one to sixty‑three by using a masked vector sequence that calculates the output size as (len/4)*3. Valid Base64 inputs are always a multiple of four bytes, so the bug only appears with malformed inputs whose length is less than four. When such an input is processed, the initial output size is zero and the padding logic decrements it, resulting in a negative output size and an incorrect output mask. The stub then writes past the logical output length before returning to Java, corrupting the heap.

The proposed fix is to add an early return to Java whenever the input length is below four, preventing the faulty calculations. The author notes that the contribution complies with the OpenJDK Interim AI Policy and that the change must not contain extraneous whitespace. The commit message must reference an issue, and the change requires at least two reviews, including one reviewer and the author. The PR is currently blocked because the referenced issue (8392044) cannot be retrieved. The description also provides commands for checking out and reviewing the pull request locally using Git or the Skara CLI tools, and a link to download the diff file. This matters because the bug can lead to heap corruption and potential security vulnerabilities when malformed Base64 data is decoded.

stories.author: jdns
stories.title: Ruby2ßhell: Pre-authentication RCE on stock Rails
stories.groq_label: Ruby versions before 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10 contain a pre‑authentication remote code execution flaw caused by a heap overflow when upcasing the character ß.
stories.groq_explain:
The page describes a security vulnerability named “Ruby2ßhell” that allows pre‑authentication remote code execution in applications that use stock Ruby on Rails. The flaw originates from Ruby’s handling of the German sharp‑s character (ß) in several single‑byte encodings such as ISO‑8859 and Windows‑125x. When a string containing ß is upcased, the code incorrectly writes two bytes while only checking space for one, leading to a one‑byte heap overflow. The overflow occurs because the output buffer is allocated with a size equal to the input length plus a small constant; each ß adds an extra byte, so an input containing 21 ß characters exceeds the buffer by one byte. The overflow writes the byte ‘S’ (or ‘s’ when case‑folding) just beyond the buffer, and an attacker can control the input length to manipulate memory and eventually read or execute arbitrary code.

The vulnerability affects Ruby versions from 2.4.0 up through the 4.0 series. Fixed releases are Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13, and 4.0.10. In default configurations the bug is reachable through the Rails framework, Sinatra in classic style, and potentially other frameworks if application code upcases strings received in a legacy encoding. UTF‑8 strings are not vulnerable because they follow a different code path.

The page also lists popular self‑hosted software that bundles an affected Ruby version. GitLab 19.6.0 (Ruby 3.3.13) and GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22.5 (Ruby 4.0.9) are marked as affected, while Mastodon 4.7.6 (Ruby 4.0.10) and OpenProject 17.9.8 (Ruby 4.0.10) are fixed. Discourse base image 2.0.20261119‑0203 and Chatwoot 4.20.0 (Ruby 3.4.4) are also affected. The recommendation is to upgrade Ruby to one of the fixed releases or install the vendor’s updated version of the affected software.

Technical details note that the same faulty loop appears in several legacy encodings and has existed since Ruby 2.4.0. The fix was applied upstream in the Ruby repository (commit d582f8f). A proof‑of‑concept exploit is being prepared for release in about a week, giving users time to apply the upgrades. The page was last updated on 19 November 2026.

stories.author: seizethecheese
stories.title: Gemini 4 Neon looks like an Opus 5.5 competitor
stories.groq_label: Gemini 4 Neon’s speed‑boosted performance is projected to be roughly on par with Opus 5.5, with a slight Elo disadvantage
stories.groq_explain:
The article discusses the newly released Gemini 4 Neon model and evaluates how its performance might compare to other top language models, particularly Opus 5.5. Gemini 4 Carbon, the previous version, holds the highest position on the author’s Agent Duel leaderboard when early voting is excluded, but it is notably slow, processing about 46 tokens per second. Gemini 4 Neon, by contrast, runs much faster—approximately 127 tokens per second when accessed through OpenRouter—while also showing incremental improvements on benchmark scores.

To assess whether Neon could be the best model overall, the author built a statistical model of the leaderboard results. The model incorporates three factors: the identity of the model, its processing speed, and whether users voted early. An interaction term between speed and early voting was added after initial attempts performed poorly, and this adjustment significantly improved the fit. The analysis suggests that speed is roughly as important as the underlying model identity in determining leaderboard rankings.

Assuming that Neon’s underlying quality is comparable to Carbon’s (or better, given its benchmark gains) and applying its faster token‑per‑second rate, the projection places Neon’s Elo rating at about 1,066. This is just below Opus 5.5’s rating of 1,078 in the author’s later snapshot of the leaderboard. The projected 90 percent confidence interval for the Elo difference ranges from –94 to +68 points, and Neon is estimated to win roughly 48.3 percent of head‑to‑head matches against Opus 5.5, counting ties as half a win.

The significance of this analysis is twofold: it highlights that the speed at which a model generates tokens can have a substantial impact on its competitive standing, and it suggests that Gemini 4 Neon may be close to matching the top‑performing Opus 5.5 despite being a newer, faster iteration of the Gemini series. This could make Neon a strong contender for the best overall model in tasks where both quality and response time matter.

stories.author: runesoerensen
stories.title: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion
stories.groq_label: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13, and 3.3.14 fix six remote code execution vulnerabilities in Regexp and string case conversion.
stories.groq_explain:
The announcement informs Ruby users that seven security flaws have been discovered in the language’s regular‑expression engine and in the case‑conversion routines for strings. All of the vulnerabilities have proof‑of‑concept exploits that can lead to remote code execution or memory corruption, and the Ruby core team has released patched versions—Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14—to address them. The advisory references the issues by their GitHub Security Advisory identifiers because CVE numbers have not yet been assigned.

The first issue (GHSA‑34m4‑m9fh‑gqp5) is a one‑byte heap buffer overflow that occurs when converting the case of a crafted string, which can be exploited for remote code execution. The second (GHSA‑7x2q‑68qv‑6p8x) is a double‑free error in regular‑expression compilation that also permits remote code execution when attacker‑controlled patterns are compiled. The third (GHSA‑87fm‑7w84‑j2px) is an integer overflow in string case conversion that leads to a heap‑based buffer overflow with similar remote execution potential. The fourth (GHSA‑wpqw‑5qxg‑m68r) is an out‑of‑bounds read in case‑insensitive regular‑expression matching, which can cause memory corruption and potentially remote code execution. The fifth (GHSA‑3p8q‑wmhx‑vm2w) is an integer overflow in the regular‑expression compiler that results in a heap buffer overflow and remote code execution. The sixth (GHSA‑7whj‑cfh7‑xgm4) is a heap buffer overflow in the Regexp#to_s method, allowing information disclosure or remote code execution when converting a crafted regular expression to a string. The seventh (GHSA‑pvgc‑g7gj‑pv6h) is an out‑of‑bounds read in case‑insensitive backreference matching that can disclose memory contents or crash the process.

Affected Ruby versions include all releases up to 3.3.13, the 3.4 series up to 3.4.12, and Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9. Users of Ruby 3.3 are still in the security‑maintenance phase, but Ruby 3.2 and earlier are end‑of‑life and will not receive these patches. The advisory strongly advises upgrading to the newly released patched versions. Credits are given to the researchers who reported the issues, including Stephan Lipp, Anthropic, baba__yaga, aphantom, Hiroya Fujinami and Hiroshi Shibata. The notice was originally published on 19 November 2026.

stories.author: ioma8
stories.title: LLM assisted reverse engineering
stories.groq_label: LLMs dramatically speed up reverse engineering by automating binary analysis with tools such as DeepSeek, Ghidra, and radare2.
stories.groq_explain:
The article is a personal account of how a two‑decade veteran of hardware and software hacking now uses large language models to accelerate reverse‑engineering tasks. The author outlines the tools, workflow, specialized agent skills, and programming choices that make the process efficient, and briefly mentions the dramatic speed‑ups achieved in recent months.

The primary tools consist of DeepSeek Harness with the DeepSeek v4.1 model for AI assistance, supplemented occasionally by Codex integrated with Luna or Terra. For static analysis the author relies on Ghidra together with the MCP bridge, which provides a free, high‑quality disassembler and decompiler that can be accessed by agents. Radare2 and the kuna CLI are also used because they are faster, though less feature‑rich than Ghidra, and they tend to work well with AI prompts.

The workflow begins by pointing an AI agent at the target binary—whether a desktop executable, website, or firmware image—and letting the agent determine the binary type, platform, and build details. The appropriate decompiler is then invoked, and the agent is instructed to document every observation in markdown files. These notes serve as personal reference, keep the agent oriented across multiple stages, and prevent the AI from wandering in circles.

After establishing a high‑level view of the binary’s main functions, control flow, and imported symbols, the author proceeds to deeper analysis. When simple disassembly or decompilation is insufficient, the agent can be commanded to debug the binary, set breakpoints, or inject probes that log runtime behavior to files. External access, such as using a desktop environment or an API‑controlled emulator for firmware, can be granted to let the agent experiment. The author emphasizes the importance of giving precise, alternative strategies— for example, directing the agent to follow string references when cross‑reference paths stall— and of monitoring the full LLM conversation to intervene when the model narrows its approach.

A set of custom “skills” enhances the agent’s capabilities. The “Matt Pottock – Grill me” skill prompts the agent to ask up to five critical clarification questions, one at a time. Specialized skills for Ghidra, radare2, or the MCP bridge encode detailed usage instructions so the agent can operate the tools without getting lost. The “hypothesis debugging” skill forces the agent to generate a testable hypothesis, log it in a CSV table, design an experiment (such as a probe or logging change), record the outcome, and repeat. This scientific‑method loop prevents endless guessing and keeps the debugging process focused.

For implementing probes or hacks, the author prefers Python with the UV tooling framework for rapid, portable scripts, and Rust for production‑grade code. Rust’s strict compiler feedback is said to give the AI immediate guidance on memory or syntax errors, despite longer compile times. The author notes that Rust has been used to build web and desktop applications, trainers, and even firmware for various embedded platforms.

Finally, the author claims that AI‑assisted reverse engineering has yielded results in the last six months that would have taken years by manual effort. Specific successes are hinted at but not detailed, indicating that the combination of large language models, advanced tooling, and disciplined agent‑driven workflows can dramatically shorten the time required to understand and modify complex binaries. This matters because it demonstrates a practical, reproducible methodology for leveraging generative AI to enhance traditional reverse‑engineering practice.

stories.author: yigitdemirag
stories.title: Gemini 4 Neon
stories.groq_label: Gemini 4 Neon is a new Google AI model offering fast, frontier‑level intelligence for complex software engineering, knowledge work, and scientific workflows.
stories.groq_explain:
Gemini 4 Neon is a new Google AI model announced on 18 November 2026 that is described as offering frontier‑level intelligence for complex software‑engineering, knowledge‑work and scientific workflows. The model can handle a 1 million‑token context window, allowing it to synthesize data from spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio and video in a single session and produce structured deliverables. It is available today through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio, the Gemini for Business product, the paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscriptions in Google Antigravity, and the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra users.

Neon is positioned as a high‑performing, production‑ready system that can run long‑running, tool‑heavy agent workflows, manage context compaction, reduce redundant file reads and act as an orchestrator for parallel sub‑agents. The model is offered at $3 per million input tokens (with a 95 percent discount for cached inputs) and $15 per million output tokens.

Benchmark results are highlighted to demonstrate its capabilities. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index Neon ranks third overall with a score of 61, second on the Vals Index and second on the new Agent Arena Index, and it is #2 for steerability in the Agent Arena. Independent evaluations place it at the top of the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench, #1 on most finance, accounting, spreadsheet‑modeling and constraint‑following benchmarks from Surge AI, and 73.5 percent on the Chartography test for reading dense professional charts. It also scores highly on Zapier’s AutomationBench, Andon Labs’ Vending‑Bench 2, and achieves the second‑highest global score on the Agent Arena Index across more than 4,200 real‑world sessions.

In scientific and mathematical reasoning Neon leads on Terminal‑Bench Science (70.5 percent), RiemannBench (84.0 percent) and HLE‑Diamond (71.3 percent). For coding tasks it ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, achieves 65.2 percent on Terminal‑Bench 4.1 and 46.2 percent on FrontierCode 2.0, and leads the mini‑SWE harness with a 12.8 percent score that triples to 39.0 percent in Google Antigravity’s testing harness.

The model offers four “thinking levels” that let teams adjust intelligence and token usage to match workload needs. At its default high setting Neon claims a 32 percent lower cost per task than the competing Carbon model while maintaining a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score, and at its highest “xhigh” setting it delivers deeper multi‑step reasoning at more than 36 percent lower cost per task than top frontier models.

Neon is also marketed for cyber‑defense applications. It produces more secure code than Carbon across easy, medium and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench, attaining state‑of‑the‑art performance on the hard tier (76 percent). In penetration‑testing benchmarks (WebExploitBench v1.2) it achieves a leading 51.26 percent score at half the cost of comparable large models, and it supports the full code‑hardening lifecycle of vulnerability finding, validation and patching.

Overall the announcement positions Gemini 4 Neon as a versatile, cost‑effective AI model that can be used for enterprise analytics, scientific research, production‑grade software development and advanced cybersecurity, marking a significant step in Google’s effort to provide powerful, controllable and safe generative AI for a wide range of professional tasks.

stories.author: de_sty
stories.title: DaisyRose-27B
stories.groq_label: DaisyRose-27B, a Qwen3.8‑27B‑based model trained with reinforcement learning on long‑horizon tasks, raises Terminal‑Bench 4.1 pass@1 to 12 % and surpasses the original model on all evaluated benchmarks.
stories.groq_explain:
The post announces the release of DaisyRose‑27B, RadixArk’s first large‑language model built on top of Qwen3.8‑27B and fine‑tuned with reinforcement learning using the open‑source Miles framework. Training focused on long‑horizon agent tasks that can involve sessions up to one million tokens. The team curated 1,200 high‑quality tasks and completed training in 18 days on a cluster of 144 H200 GPUs. The new model improves the Terminal‑Bench 4.1 pass@1 score from 5.6 percent to 12.0 percent and shows gains on a variety of reasoning, instruction‑following, and coding benchmarks. Checkpoints are provided in BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 formats for public use.

Three main factors are credited for the performance gains. First, the training data were created in partnership with Eigent AI. Thousands of candidate tasks from machine‑learning, software engineering, science and other domains were evaluated, and about 1,200 were selected because each one exposed a specific mistake made by the original Qwen3.8‑27B model. Tasks were designed as long chains of interdependent problems, requiring an agent to plan, reason and execute over many tool calls, with sandbox runs limited to 1.5 hours, more than 100 tool calls and up to 256 k output tokens. All tasks were reviewed to prevent reward‑hacking and to ensure genuine problem solving.

Second, the training backend was optimized for efficiency. Miles runs in a fully asynchronous mode where agents continue to generate trajectories while the model updates, using 128 GPUs for inference and 16 GPUs for training. The system achieved a model FLOPs utilization of 37 percent, compared with about 16 percent for a comparable open‑source trainer built on Megatron, resulting in a 57 percent reduction in GPU time. For mixture‑of‑experts models the speedup was even larger. The overall training ran at roughly 16 800 tokens per second across the 144 GPUs, twice the speed of the open‑source baseline, and maintained stable performance over the nine‑week, 63 000 GPU‑hour run.

Third, a robust sandbox service was used to evaluate every agent attempt. Built on the open‑source AgentENV project, the service executed about 944 000 sandbox instances, sometimes running as many as 1 566 simultaneously, with a success rate above 99 percent and later exceeding 99.95 percent. The infrastructure dynamically allocated memory to each sandbox, cutting cloud sandbox costs by roughly 80 percent relative to popular providers.

The team invites users to download DaisyRose‑27B from Hugging Face and to experiment with their own agents using Miles. They emphasize that the approach of combining high‑quality data with efficient infrastructure can be applied to specialized models while preserving broader capabilities. The post concludes with acknowledgments to Eigent AI, the Qwen team, and various open‑source communities, and notes that evaluation was performed on the Terminal‑Bench benchmark.

stories.author: leumon
stories.title: Genie 4 is now available
stories.groq_label: Google releases Genie 4 adding real time world editing native audio and a new creation agent for Project Genie Ultra subscribers
stories.groq_explain:
The article announces that Genie 4 is now available as part of a refreshed Project Genie experience for Google AI Ultra subscribers. The rollout adds the newest world model, Genie 4, along with upgrades to Genie 3, a new Project Genie agent, and a community gallery where users can discover, explore, and remix interactive worlds.

Genie 4 is described as the most realistic and interactive world model released by Google DeepMind. It lets users modify their environments in real time by typing new prompts while navigating a world, allowing changes to weather, characters, or actions on the fly. The model also introduces native audio that adapts dynamically to the visual scene, providing ambient soundscapes and character dialogue that evolve as the user explores.

Genie 3 remains available for longer sessions and for generating panoramas. The updated Genie 3 now supports three‑minute generations instead of sixty seconds, the ability to chain multiple worlds together for extended journeys, grounding of new worlds from 360‑degree panorama images, and real‑time in‑world events triggered by natural‑language prompts.

The Project Genie agent expands creation beyond single prompts. Users can describe a vision in natural language and the agent coordinates Google’s multimodal models to produce initial visuals, a signature aesthetic, and custom background music. Gemini models can be integrated into the session to observe the screen, offer context‑aware suggestions, and automatically trigger events.

A new gallery showcases curated worlds and community creations. Examples include “Living Memory,” which turns personal photos into explorable spaces; “Dino Field Guide,” a prehistoric habitat built from 360‑degree panoramas; and “Rock Paper Scissors,” where Gemini acts as a real‑time referee. Collaborative projects such as “Villa Giallo,” a gothic manor mystery created with technologist Will (BLVCKL!GHT), and “The Life of Ants,” a colony exploration built with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, demonstrate the capabilities of Genie 4’s photorealism.

The article emphasizes responsible development. All generated video and audio are watermarked with SynthID, and inputs and outputs undergo safety screenings. Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain frontier research models, and Google is actively addressing challenges like camera latency, complex physical interactions, precise real‑time audio, and long‑term scene permanence. A link to a Genie 4 model research overview is provided for further details.

Eligibility is limited to Google AI Ultra subscribers, who can start using the new Project Genie experience immediately. Google AI Pro members may join a waitlist. The page also offers a newsletter signup for product updates and related news.

stories.author: aray07
stories.title: The Magic of Partial Evaluation
stories.groq_label: Partial evaluation precomputes known inputs at compile time, generating specialized code that eliminates unnecessary runtime computation.
stories.groq_explain:
The article is a personal essay about the elegance of partial evaluation, a technique that separates the parts of a program that can be computed at compile time from those that must wait until runtime. The author begins by describing a fascination with software ideas that are beautiful in themselves, even if they lack immediate practical use, and explains that programming languages are a particular obsession because they allow solving whole classes of problems by stepping back to the meta‑level.

Partial evaluation is introduced through simple JavaScript examples. The factorial function called with a constant argument is shown to be fully reducible to the constant product 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1, meaning a sufficiently clever compiler could compute the result at build time and emit only the final value. A second example with a recursive power function where the base comes from the command line demonstrates how the same idea can reduce a program to a form that contains only the dynamic pieces (the unknown base) while eliminating the recursion.

The “big idea” is that a partial evaluator executes whatever can be determined statically and leaves the rest untouched. The author illustrates this with a tiny arithmetic interpreter that evaluates expression trees. When all operands are known, the interpreter collapses the whole tree to a single number. When a leaf contains an unknown value (e.g., `Number(process.argv[2])`), the evaluator still simplifies the surrounding structure, ending with an expression that mixes the unknown value with the computed constant part.

The piece then moves to a more ambitious example: a Brainfuck interpreter written in JavaScript. The author starts showing the code that sets up the tape, jump‑table, and pointer handling, hinting that partial evaluation can be applied to such an interpreter to generate a specialized, faster version—effectively turning the interpreter into a compiler for the specific Brainfuck program.

The motivation for writing the article stems from James Long’s revival of Meta’s JavaScript partial evaluator called Prepack. The author notes that Prepack prioritized practicality over beauty, which prompted a personal effort to create a new library that emphasizes the aesthetic and educational aspects of partial evaluation rather than production use.

Overall, the article explains what partial evaluation is, demonstrates its mechanics with concrete JavaScript snippets, and argues that the technique reveals deep connections between interpreters and compilers. It matters because it shows how reasoning about static and dynamic parts of a program can lead to automatic generation of optimized code, providing insight into language design and the nature of computation. The content ends part‑way through the Brainfuck example, so the full implementation and further discussion are not present. However, the existing text makes clear the author’s enthusiasm for partial evaluation and its potential to turn interpreters into “free” compilers.

stories.author: mooreds
stories.title: Scottish HTTP Codes
stories.groq_label: A humorous list of Scottish‑styled reinterpretations of HTTP status codes
stories.groq_explain: The page titled “Scottish HTTP Codes” is a tongue‑in‑cheek list that pairs standard HTTP status numbers with colourful Scots‑language phrases, many of which contain profanity. Each numeric code is followed by a short, often vulgar, colloquial expression meant to convey the same idea as the official status message but in a distinctly Scottish dialect. For example, 100 is rendered as “AYE, HAUD ON,” 200 becomes “NAE BOTHER,” 301 is “AWAY OWER THERE,” 404 is expressed as “NAE FUCKIN HERE, PAL,” and 500 appears as “AH’VE FUCKED IT.” The list covers a range of common client‑error, redirection, and server‑error codes such as 301, 302, 304, 307, 308, 400 through 425, 429, 431, 451, 500 through 505, and even the less usual 418 (“AH’M A FUCKIN TEAPOT”). The content is purely humorous, providing a cultural remix of technical status codes rather than any functional specification. Its significance lies in its playful use of regional slang to humanise and satirise internet protocol language, illustrating how technical jargon can be reimagined for comedic effect.
